<reason>PRO built the cleaner path to victory. Its core reframe ("the curb is already priced; the question is who pays") was never dislodged, and it progressively narrowed the clash to a single question: how is a bay allocated when lawful demand exceeds supply at zero price? CON's answers evolved from "rules and enforcement" to a late request-order reservation queue, which PRO punctured in closing (at zero price the flexible van has no reason to shift; the queue is just moved online). CON's honest concession that scarcity remains under either policy when all trips are inflexible handed PRO the "tie in the worst case, win everywhere else" weighing, and PRO's stress on the motion's permissive "allow" wording lowered its burden effectively. CON landed real hits—the "few cents" vs. effectiveness tension, ability-to-pay ≠ necessity, rules can vary by time of day—and stayed epistemically disciplined, but its case was mostly defensive and never gave a positive reason cities should be forbidden the dial. PRO's two clipped turns are a minor execution cost that does not offset its clearer comparison.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's A1 in Turn 7 answering CON's cap-or-raise dilemma: the price rises until the marginal flexible stop leaves, inflexible vans queue anyway under CON's system at greater idling cost, cities may cap or exempt, and the motion says "allow." Combined with the closing's dismantling of CON's free reservation queue, this neutralized CON's strongest pressure and set the decisive weighing.</best_rebuttal>
